Measure at consistent times, rest and sit correctly, use the right cuff size, and keep a record. If you've never checked at home, pick up a validated monitor, set aside a week, and share the results with your healthcare provider.

*This article is for general information only and isn't a substitute for professional medical advice. Talk with your healthcare provider about the monitoring schedule and targets that are right for you.*

# Language Programmes at East Otago High School

Learning a language changes how you see the world. It brings new words, new ways of thinking, new relationships, and a deeper understanding of the people around you. At East Otago High School (EOHS), our programmes in **Te Reo Māori** and **German** grow with students from Year 7 through to Year 10, and each stage has its own purpose.

> **Note:** Details in square brackets, such as lesson hours and textbook titles, are placeholders to be confirmed with the Languages department before publication.

## Why Two Languages?

**Te Reo Māori** is an official language of Aotearoa New Zealand and a taonga (treasure) of this land. Learning it connects students to the history, people, and places of their community, including the iwi and hapū of the East Otago coast.

**German** opens a window onto Europe. It is a major language of science, engineering, music, and tourism, and it shows students how to approach a language that shares roots with English but follows its own rules.

Together, they let students develop a strong local identity alongside a global outlook.

## Years 7 and 8: Cultural Introduction

Junior students take both languages on a rotating or concurrent basis, typically **[X lessons per week / X hours per term]**. The aim is exposure and enjoyment rather than intensive study.

**Te Reo Māori** focuses on everyday language and tikanga (customs). Students learn:

- Greetings, introductions, and simple conversational phrases
- Their own pepeha, a formal introduction connecting a person to their maunga (mountain), awa (river), and whakapapa (ancestry)
- Waiata (songs) and karakia (prayers or blessings) used in school and community settings
- Key concepts such as manaakitanga (hospitality and care), whanaungatanga (relationships), and kaitiakitanga (guardianship)

Students also meet the **Kāi Tahu dialect** of Te Waipounamu (the South Island), in which "k" often replaces "ng", so they say *Kāi Tahu* rather than *Ngāi Tahu*. This shows them that Te Reo Māori is a living language rooted in place.

**German** is a taster course covering greetings, numbers, colours, and the alphabet; family, pets, and describing yourself; food and festivals such as Christmas markets and Oktoberfest; and the basic geography of Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Lessons are active and playful, with games, songs, and short role-plays.

Classes use **[textbook/resource title for Te Reo Māori]** and **[textbook/resource title for German]**, plus teacher-made materials, digital tools, and audio resources.

The main goal is cultural introduction. Students should finish Year 8 curious, confident with basic phrases, and aware that every language carries a culture with it.

## Year 9: Building Foundations

Languages become more structured, with **[X lessons per week]**. Depending on timetabling, students may choose to focus on one language.

**Te Reo Māori** students build grammar and vocabulary more systematically. Themes include whānau (family) and home life, kai (food) and hospitality, the school and local environment, and pūrākau (traditional stories), including those connected to the Otago coastline. Students begin forming their own sentences, using patterns such as *He aha tēnei?* (What is this?), and reading short texts.

**German** moves beyond the basics to school life and daily routines, hobbies, sport and free time, shopping and money, and telling the time and making arrangements. Students are introduced to key grammar: noun genders, verb conjugation, and word order.

Resources are **[Year 9 textbook titles]**, workbooks, and online practice platforms.

## Year 10: Preparing for the Next Step

Year 10 language is usually an option subject, with **[X lessons per week]**. Students who choose it are generally considering further study, so the pace and expectations increase.

**Te Reo Māori** prepares students for **NCEA Level 1** while building practical community skills. Themes include describing people, places, and events in more detail; past, present, and future tenses; formal language for speeches and ceremonies; and marae tikanga, including pōwhiri (welcome ceremonies), roles on the marae, and appropriate behaviour.

A distinctive goal is **local marae liaison**. Students learn the language and protocols needed to take part respectfully in marae events. Some may support school pōwhiri, help welcome visitors, or represent EOHS on community occasions, building strong relationships between the school and local mana whenua.

**German** has two practical aims: preparing students for **NCEA German** and giving them the language to **travel** in German-speaking countries. Themes include travel and transport, accommodation and directions, ordering food and handling everyday situations, and comparing life in New Zealand with life in Germany, Austria, or Switzerland. Students practise writing short texts, holding conversations, and understanding authentic material such as menus, signs, and timetables.

Resources are **[Year 10 textbook titles]** and NCEA-aligned practice tasks.

## Summary at a Glance

| Level | Te Reo Māori Focus | German Focus | Main Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Years 7–8 | Greetings, pepeha, waiata, tikanga | Basics, family, food, festivals | Cultural introduction |
| Year 9 | Whānau, kai, local pūrākau | School, hobbies, shopping | Building foundations |
| Year 10 | Formal language, marae tikanga | Travel, everyday situations | NCEA preparation, travel, marae liaison |

## Looking Ahead

Students who continue beyond Year 10 can work towards NCEA credits and, ultimately, University Entrance. Just as importantly, they leave with lasting skills: confidence in speaking, respect for other cultures, and a stronger connection to their own community.

Whether a student wants to stand with confidence on a local marae or order a meal in a Berlin café, the language programmes at East Otago High School are designed to help them get there, one word at a time.

*Kia kaha te reo. Viel Erfolg!*
